query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 0.2 atomic percent molybdenum (Mo) during alloy synthesis will enhance the mechanical performance and corrosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a dual-phase (fcc/B2 or L12/B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy chemistry by incorporating 0.2 at.% Mo during melting/casting to produce an AlCoCrFeNi2.1Mo0.2 alloy.
generation.conditions: Fastener components are to be evaluated under service-relevant cyclic temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, ambient (room-temperature) creep conditions, and corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing solutions) that simulate engine or coastal applications.
generation.structural_mediator: An optimized lamellar microstructure with a refined phase fraction between the ductile fcc (or L12) and the hard B2 phases, where Mo incorporation helps stabilize the phase boundary and fine-scale composite architecture.
generation.mechanism: The Mo addition is expected to modify the phase balance and interface chemistry. It refines and stabilizes the lamellar dual-phase structure by enhancing the two-hierarchical constraint and microcrack-arresting mechanisms, thereby improving the alloy’s strength, ductility, and resistance to creep and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-modified alloy will exhibit increased yield and tensile strengths along with an improved fracture elongation and better corrosion resistance compared to the original alloy. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be within the range observed in similar alloying studies, though precise values remain to be quantified.
generation.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without any Mo addition.
generation.boundary: The enhanced performance is applicable for fasteners operating under extreme temperature cycling, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep conditions, and corrosive exposures typical of industrial applications (such as in aerospace or marine environments).
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies suggest Mo can beneficially modify mechanical and corrosion properties, the exact percentage improvement and preservation of ductility under all testing regimes remain uncertain until verified by controlled experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of fastener component samples from the same processing batch: (a) the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and (b) the Mo-modified AlCoCrFeNi2.1Mo0.2 alloy. Process both identically (same casting and thermo-mechanical treatment) and subject them to a series of tests simulating extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and exposure to corrosive media.
measurements: Tensile tests (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Corrosion tests in representative chloride-containing environments
Microstructural analysis (via SEM/TEM and phase identification) before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo0.2-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical properties (strength and ductility), creep resistance, and corrosion behavior relative to the baseline alloy under the defined testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Due to their unique solid solution structures, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) typically exhibit various excellent properties, such as high strength/hardness [,,,], high wear resistance [], outstanding temperature strength [], strong structural stability [], good corrosion resistance [,], and oxidation resistance [] Generally speaking, HEAs can be divided into face-centered cubic (FCC) HEAs, body-centered cubic (BCC) HEAs, FCC + BCC two-phase HEAs, etc., from the perspective of phase structure. The high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a single FCC structure has high ductility but low hardness. For example, the CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a room temperature fracture elongation of 52%, but a tensile strength of only 563 MPa [], and the Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy has a tensile ductility of 58%, but a yield strength of only 240 MPa []. Although HEA with a single BCC structure has high strength and hardness, it also has low ductility. Therefore, an important challenge in the engineering application of high-entropy alloys is how to obtain high strength and high ductility at the same time. Figure 4a shows the stress–strain curves and corresponding fracture morphologies of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1Xy (X = V, Mo, B; y = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3) EHEAs. The tensile strength of the alloys increases and then decreases with the increase in the high-melting-point metals V and Mo, which results from the change in the ratio of the FCC phase to the BCC phase in these alloys. The mechanical properties of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1Xy alloy are more affected by changes in the B contents compared with the V and Mo. The tensile strength of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1By alloy decreases significantly with increasing B elements, and the best mechanical properties were found in the B0.1 alloy. The tensile property of the Mo0.2 alloy is superior to that of the other two alloys with different contents. The tensile strength of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy is greatly increased after adding 0.2 at.% Mo, while the alloy still retains a fracture elongation of more than 24%, as listed in Table 2. The Mo0.2 alloy presents the maximum strength and plasticity when compared to other types of eutectic high-entropy alloy. Its tensile strength is enhanced by 3.6~34%, and its fracture elongation is raised by 0.9~2.9 times.
